claims.claim: Hesychius of Jerusalem was a Christian priest (presbyter) and exegete active during the first half of the fifth century.
According to Theophanes Confessor, Hesychius became presbyter at Jerusalem in 412.
Hesychius was recognized by 429 as the pre-eminent biblical interpreter and teacher of the church in Jerusalem and Palestine.
The work In sanctum Lucam (Homily 21) is dubiously attributed to Hesychius of Jerusalem and is considered misattributed by modern scholarship.
The homily is a late 5th to 7th century Greek work, making it the earliest extant source for Saint Luke's feast on 18 October.
The text stresses Luke's role as source of our knowledge about Mary, the Mother of Christ.
The homily contains a biographical note stating Luke was a physician of Syrian origin, a disciple of the Apostles and follower of Paul, who died at Thebes of Boeotia at age 84 on 18 October.
The work survives in manuscript tradition and was edited in Migne's Patrologia Graeca (PG 93) under Hesychius' name, though its authenticity is disputed.
A comprehensive critical edition of the homilies transmitted under Hesychius' name, both authentic and spurious, was published by Michel Aubineau.
The homily matters as the earliest extant witness to the liturgical commemoration of Saint Luke on 18 October and for its emphasis on Luke's unique contributions to Marian traditions.
